lessons.plain: A project is a piece of work with a clear beginning and end that makes something new, such as a new office network or a new app release. Unlike routine work that repeats every day, a project is temporary and aims at a unique result. Project characteristics are the features that make something a project rather than ongoing operations, and they help you decide how to run it. Methodologies are the overall styles of managing a project, such as planning everything first or delivering in short rounds. The right style depends on how well the goal is understood at the start.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has been asked to replace the company's email server by the end of next quarter, and the work is finished once the switch is done. Another team checks the backups every night, indefinitely. Which of these two pieces of work is a project, and what single feature tells you that?
lessons.teach:
A project is temporary work that produces a unique result, with a defined start and a defined end. Temporary means it has a finish point. Unique means the result has not been produced in exactly this form before. Operations is different: it is ongoing, repeating work, such as checking backups every night. Projects are often planned roughly at first and refined as the team learns more. This is called progressive elaboration. Near-term work gets detailed planning, while later work stays broad until more is known.

Projects are judged against constraints, the limits that pull against each other: scope (what is delivered), schedule (when it is delivered), cost (how much it costs), and quality and resources (the standard expected and the people and tools available). Changing one usually affects another. A methodology is the overall approach used to run the project. A predictive methodology plans most of the work up front and then carries it out in order, which suits goals that are well understood. An adaptive methodology works in short cycles and revisits the plan after each one, which suits goals that will change as they are learned. A hybrid approach mixes the two.

Worked example: a team must move 400 staff mailboxes to a new email system by 30 June. Step one: confirm it is a project, since it has a start, a finish, and produces a new setup. Step two: note the constraints. The date is fixed, so if the work runs late, scope or cost must give way. Step three: choose a method. The migration steps are well known, so a predictive plan with a fixed sequence fits.

Common mistake: calling ongoing support a project because it is important, then closing it when a deadline passes and leaving nobody responsible for it. In a running system, that means an on-call duty with no owner the day after the project closes.

A project ends when its goal is met, and the result is handed over to operations, where someone owns it day to day.

questions.prompt: A county library service is adding a reading-room feature to its catalogue website. Its requirements are still being found out through user sessions, and the team expects the list to change after each round of feedback. Step one: confirm it is a project, because it has a start, a finish, and produces a new feature. Step two: note the constraints. The launch date is fixed for the start of the autumn term, so if testing runs late, scope has to give way. Step three is missing. Which choice correctly completes the method decision?
choices: Operations, because the feature will run on the existing web servers once it is switched on
Hybrid, because the project has a finish date and the team also has to keep the site running
Predictive, because a fixed up-front plan protects the launch date and the requirements are already known
Adaptive, because short cycles with a plan review after each one suit goals that will shift as users are observed
questions.why: Requirements that will change as they are learned call for an adaptive methodology, which works in short cycles and revisits the plan after each one, so the other choices misapply predictive, operations, or hybrid thinking.

questions.prompt: A freight company is rolling out handheld barcode scanners to 12 warehouses, a one-time change with a set finish. Afterwards, staff will reconcile stock counts every night as routine work. Which statement is correct?
choices: Neither is a project, because both involve the same warehouse staff
Both the rollout and the nightly reconciliation are projects, because both involve scanners
The rollout is a project because it is temporary and produces a unique result, and the nightly reconciliation is operations because it is ongoing and repeating
The nightly reconciliation is a project because it is important, and the rollout is operations
questions.why: A project is temporary and produces a unique result, while operations is ongoing, repeating work, so the one-time rollout is a project and the nightly reconciliation is operations.

questions.prompt: A museum's ticketing upgrade has a fixed launch date and a fixed budget. Midway through, the sponsor asks for two more features, and the quality standard stays the same. What is the most accurate reading of the constraints?
choices: Adding features is free as long as the team works longer hours, because scope is the only constraint that matters
Scope, schedule, cost, and quality pull against each other, so adding scope means the schedule, cost, or resources must change, or scope must be cut elsewhere
The constraints are independent, so the team can add features without any other change
The launch date will move automatically because the sponsor is paying for the change
questions.why: Scope, schedule, cost, and quality are linked, so extra features under a fixed date and budget force a trade-off or a resource change, and the other choices ignore that link.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm finishes building an invoice-approval workflow and the project's goal is met. The team disbands the next day and nobody is named to check the nightly approval job. Which action best reflects how the project should have closed?
choices: The project should have been closed as soon as the workflow was built, before the goal was checked
The nightly job should have been treated as a new project with its own start and end dates
The project should have been closed once its goal was met, with the result handed to operations and a named day-to-day owner
The project should have stayed open indefinitely until someone volunteered to own the nightly job
questions.why: A project ends when its goal is met and the result is handed to operations, where someone owns it day to day, so the closing step should have included naming that owner.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a piece of work is a project or ongoing operations, and how that distinction affects the way you choose a delivery method. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I check whether the work has a defined end and whether the result is new or unique. If it finishes when a goal is met, it is a project, and if it repeats indefinitely, it is operations. That matters for method because a project with a well-understood goal and fixed steps suits a predictive plan, while one where the goal will shift as we learn suits short adaptive cycles. The limit is that some work is hard to classify. A service rollout may have a project phase and then an operations phase, so I would define the handover point early, so the team knows who owns the result once the project closes.
rubricPoints: Defines a project as temporary with a defined end and a unique result
Contrasts projects with repeating ongoing operations
Links the characteristics to choosing predictive, adaptive, or hybrid methods
Names a limit, such as blurred boundaries or the need for a clear handover

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly definitions and classification, which a clear reading with a worked example covers well without a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: Projects can be run in two broad ways. Waterfall plans the whole job up front, finishes each stage in order (requirements, design, build, test, release), and only then moves on. Agile breaks the work into short cycles, usually one to four weeks long, and delivers a working slice at the end of each cycle so that feedback can change what comes next. Neither approach is better everywhere. Waterfall suits work where requirements are fixed and late changes are costly. Agile suits work where the goal is clear but the best solution is still unknown. A project manager's job is to match the approach to the uncertainty and the constraints.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is building a new dispatch screen for a vehicle fleet, and the buyers cannot yet say exactly what the screen should show. Would you plan every screen on paper before any coding starts, or release a rough version every two weeks and adjust based on what people do with it? Why?
lessons.teach:
Waterfall is a sequential approach. Work moves through phases such as requirements, design, build, test and release, and each phase is signed off before the next begins. Its strength is predictability: scope, cost and schedule are estimated early, and changes after sign-off are expensive. It fits work with stable requirements, such as an integration that a regulator has already specified in detail.

Agile is an iterative approach. Work is split into short timeboxes called sprints, typically one to four weeks. Each sprint produces a small working increment that stakeholders (the people who use or fund the work) can inspect. The prioritized list of remaining work is called the backlog, and it is reordered as learning arrives. Scrum is one common agile framework, with defined roles and recurring events such as a sprint review.

Worked example: a team must replace a legacy depot-scheduling tool. Step 1: the sponsor is unsure whether dispatchers want drag-and-drop or list views. Step 2: under agile, the team ships a list view in sprint 1 and watches dispatchers use it. Step 3: feedback shows they want filters by shift, so the backlog is reordered. Step 4: the drag-and-drop idea is dropped before effort is wasted on it. Under waterfall, the same discovery would arrive only after the full design had been built and signed off.

Common mistake: calling a project agile because it has weekly meetings, or choosing agile where requirements are fixed in advance and cannot legitimately change.

In a running system, a waterfall release can ship months of untested assumptions at once, so a rollback is large and risky. Agile releases smaller increments, which are easier to test and to reverse.

questions.prompt: A credit union must update its online loan application form. A banking regulator has already issued the exact list of required fields in writing, so the requirements are stable, and the team chooses a waterfall approach, meaning it completes each phase and gets sign-off before starting the next. Step 1: the design is completed and signed off by the sponsor. Step 2: the build is completed and signed off. Step 3: after sign-off, a compliance officer asks for one extra field to be added to the form. Step 4 is missing. Which step should the project manager take next, before agreeing to build the extra field?
choices: Estimate how much the late change will add to the cost and schedule, because changes after sign-off are expensive under waterfall, and get that impact accepted before rebuilding.
Release the form now without the field and schedule a separate project for it later.
Ask the team to start an agile sprint so the new field can be added and tested as a one-week increment.
Add the field in the current build without telling anyone, since the change is small.
questions.why: Under waterfall, changes after sign-off are expensive, so the project manager must first assess the cost and schedule effect of the late change and get it accepted before rework begins.

questions.prompt: A warehouse operator is replacing its stock-counting handheld app. Staff have never used a digital version, so nobody can say which screens they will need. Which approach fits this work best?
choices: Waterfall, because the team should sign off a complete design before any staff see the app.
Agile, because short sprints that produce a working increment let staff use early versions and shape the backlog as they learn.
Waterfall, because agile cannot be used for any mobile application.
Neither approach, because the project should be cancelled until requirements are fixed.
questions.why: When requirements are unknown and learning from users is needed, agile's short sprints and reorderable backlog fit best; the other options misread either approach.

questions.prompt: A school district's payroll team is building a system that must apply tax tables published by the government in fixed form, with no room for interpretation. A colleague argues the project should be agile because the team will hold short daily check-in meetings. What is the best response?
choices: Disagree on the meetings, but agree on agile because the district's requirements will change every sprint.
Disagree, because payroll projects cannot be run with any formal approach.
Agreed, because daily meetings are the defining feature of agile work.
Disagree, because holding meetings does not make a project agile, and fixed, specified requirements suit a waterfall approach.
questions.why: Calling a project agile because of meetings is a common mistake, and fixed published requirements point toward waterfall, so the best answer rejects the colleague's reasoning and the stated reason for agile.

questions.prompt: A regional bank runs a six-month waterfall project and releases all of it in one go. Two weeks after go-live, a flaw is found in an assumption made in month two. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: The team can roll back one sprint's worth of change, which takes a day.
Rolling back is large and risky, because months of untested assumptions shipped together.
The flaw is small and easy to reverse, because the team only changed one screen.
The flaw has no effect, because waterfall tests each phase separately before release.
questions.why: A waterfall release bundles months of work, so a single bad assumption is hard to isolate, and a rollback touches a large amount of the running system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only worked on waterfall projects how an agile project would handle a stakeholder asking, halfway through, to change the scope. Name one limit or tradeoff of the agile approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: In waterfall, a mid-project scope change goes through a formal change request, because the plan and budget were locked at sign-off. The change must be re-estimated and re-approved, and the schedule may slip. In agile, the request goes into the product backlog. The product owner, who orders the backlog, decides whether it beats the items already queued, and if so it is scheduled into a future sprint without reopening the whole plan. The tradeoff is that agile gives less up-front certainty. The final scope, total cost and completion date are not fixed, so stakeholders must accept a forecast that moves as they learn. The approach also depends on stakeholders attending reviews. Without that, the backlog drifts and changes are never really judged.
rubricPoints: Waterfall handles scope changes through formal re-approval because the plan was fixed at sign-off.
Agile adds the request to a prioritized backlog and schedules it into a future sprint.
A named tradeoff: agile gives less certainty about final scope, cost or date.
Agile needs active stakeholder involvement, or the backlog loses meaning.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner work through Agile and Scrum practice, which directly exercises the difference between iterative and sequential delivery.

lessons.plain: Change control is the agreed routine a project uses to decide whether a change to its scope, schedule, budget or deliverables should happen, and to record what changed. Projects drift constantly: a customer asks for one more feature, a supplier delivers late, a rule changes. Without a process, these changes slip in unnoticed and the team ends up with a plan nobody can trust. Change control gives every request the same path: write it down, estimate its effects, decide, then update the plan and tell people. Think of it like a logbook at a ship's gate that every change must be signed into before anything is loaded.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor says, 'Just add the export button, it's only a small thing, and we'll sort out the paperwork later.' Before you know anything else about the project, what could go wrong with saying yes straight away, and what would you want to check first?
lessons.teach:
A change request is a formal written proposal to alter something the project has already agreed on. The baseline is the approved version of scope, schedule and cost that the project is measured against. A change control board (CCB) is the group of stakeholders who approve or reject changes. Impact analysis is the estimate of how a change affects scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk.

Change control works because every change is a trade-off. Adding work usually costs time or money, or it pushes something else out. The process forces that trade-off into view before anyone commits effort.

Worked example: a customer asks to add a live-map export feature to a fleet-tracking project. Step 1: log change request CR-14 with a description and the reason. Step 2: the project manager runs impact analysis and finds three developer weeks of work, a two-week delay to user acceptance testing, and extra cost. Step 3: the CCB reviews it and chooses to approve, defer to a later phase, or reject. Step 4: if approved, the baseline and schedule are updated, the decision is recorded, and the team is told what changed.

Common mistake: agreeing to a change verbally and starting the work before anyone approves it. The baseline then no longer matches what is being built.

In a running system the effect is concrete. If a configuration change reaches production without a recorded change request, the next incident is hard to trace, because nobody can say which version was live or why it changed. Change control is the record that makes that question answerable.

questions.prompt: A regional library network runs a project to replace its catalogue system. A branch manager submits change request CR-07 asking for a self-service holds shelf, reasoning that patrons keep asking for it. Step 1: CR-07 is logged with the description and reason. Step 2: the project manager runs impact analysis and finds four days of developer work, no change to the go-live date, and a licence cost of 900 dollars. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: if approved, the baseline and schedule are updated, the decision is recorded, and the team is told what changed. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The project sponsor updates the baseline to include the holds shelf before any review takes place.
The change control board reviews the impact analysis and decides to approve, defer, or reject CR-07.
The developer starts building the holds shelf during the current sprint so it is ready when the request is approved.
The change request is closed as complete because the impact analysis has already been written.
questions.why: Step 3 is the board's decision on the request, based on the impact analysis, and it must happen before the baseline is changed or any work is authorised.

questions.prompt: A warehouse inventory project has an approved scope, a schedule ending in June, and a budget of 240,000 dollars. The team later wants to compare actual progress against what was agreed. Which item is the baseline the project is measured against?
choices: The current forecast, which is updated each week by the project manager from new estimates.
The notes from the sponsor's kickoff call, which record the informal priorities discussed.
The approved version of scope, schedule and cost, which the project is measured against.
The list of ideas the team raised during the first workshop, before anything was approved.
questions.why: The baseline is defined as the approved version of scope, schedule and cost, so it is the agreed reference point, not a forecast or informal notes.

questions.prompt: A developer at a university course-portal project changes a database index directly on the live server after a colleague mentions it informally in a meeting. No change request is logged. Two weeks later, a report slows down and the team cannot tell which configuration was live on the day the slowdown began. What is the core problem?
choices: The developer did not test the change in a separate environment, so the slowdown was caused by the test gap.
No formal record exists of the change, so nobody can establish which version was live or why it changed.
The index change cost more than the project budget allowed, which caused the slowdown to appear.
The change board was not given enough time to review the index change before it went live.
questions.why: Change control keeps a record of each approved change, and without a logged request the team cannot trace which configuration was in place or why it changed.

questions.prompt: A course-portal project receives change request CR-22 asking to add a grade export. The impact analysis finds three days of work, no delay to the schedule, no added cost, and a small risk that the export could expose student data if misconfigured. Who should decide whether CR-22 goes ahead?
choices: The customer's IT help desk, because it is the group that will later support the export feature.
The lead developer, because the work is small and the developer will do it anyway.
The change control board, which weighs the impact analysis and makes the approve, defer, or reject decision.
The project manager alone, because impact analysis is the project manager's sole responsibility.
questions.why: The change control board is the group of stakeholders responsible for approving or rejecting changes, and it decides after impact analysis is complete, even when the change looks small.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why even a small change should go through change control, and name one limit or trade-off of making the process strict.
lessons.modelAnswer: A small change still matters because it alters the baseline, and small changes add up. If each one is agreed informally, the schedule and budget drift without anyone seeing it, and the team cannot say later what was approved. Change control makes a change visible: someone writes the request down, the impact on scope, schedule and cost is estimated, and an approver decides. The trade-off is speed. A strict process can slow down urgent or low-risk fixes, so teams often agree a lighter fast path for minor changes while keeping a record of them. The aim is traceability without turning every small tweak into a committee meeting.
rubricPoints: Defines change control as a formal process for approving and recording changes to the baseline.
Explains that small changes accumulate and can erode schedule, budget or scope if untracked.
Mentions impact analysis as the estimate of effects before a decision.
Names a real trade-off, such as slower decisions or delayed urgent fixes, and a way to manage it.

suggested.rationale: A change request moving through states such as submitted, assessed, approved or rejected, with the baseline updated only on approval, is a state machine that learners can practise directly.

lessons.plain: Risk management means looking ahead at things that might go wrong on a project, deciding how much they matter, and choosing what to do about them before they happen. A risk is a possible event, not a certainty: a supplier might be late, a key person might leave, or a new rule might change what you are building. Good project managers write risks down, estimate how likely and how painful each one is, and plan a response while acting is still cheap. It is like checking the weather and packing an umbrella before you leave, rather than getting soaked and then looking for shelter.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team is building a mobile app, and the only developer who knows the payment library might leave for another job next month. Before reading anything, what would you do about this, and how would you decide whether it deserves attention compared with the other things on your list?
lessons.teach:
A risk is an uncertain event that, if it happens, would affect one or more project objectives such as scope, schedule, cost or quality. Uncertain is the key word: a risk has not happened yet. Once it happens it becomes an issue, which is handled separately. Each risk has a probability (how likely it is, often rated low, medium or high) and an impact (how much harm it would cause if it occurred). Combining the two gives a rough priority, sometimes called a risk score. The team records risks in a risk register, a living list that holds each risk, its score, a named owner who watches it, and the chosen response.

There are four standard responses to a threat. Avoid means change the plan so the risk cannot occur. Transfer means shift the consequence to someone else, usually through insurance or a contract clause. Mitigate means reduce the probability or the impact, for example by cross-training a second developer. Accept means acknowledge the risk and watch it, sometimes with a contingency reserve of time or money set aside. Escalate means pass a risk to a sponsor when it exceeds what the team is allowed to decide. Positive uncertainties, called opportunities, have their own parallel responses.

Worked example: the payment-library developer. The probability is medium, since people change jobs often. The impact is high, because nobody else can fix payment bugs. The score is high, so it is a priority. The owner, the team lead, chooses to mitigate: she pairs a second developer on the library this sprint and writes a short guide. The residual risk, the risk left after the response, is now low, and she records that in the register.

A common mistake is writing risks as vague fears such as things could go wrong, with no owner, no score and no response. Another is calling a problem that has already happened a risk. When a risk is ignored, the team discovers it only as an issue, at a higher cost.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank is running a volunteer scheduling project. One risk is that its volunteer coordinator may leave before the spring drive. The team rates the probability as high and the impact as medium, so the combined score is high and the risk is a priority. The operations lead, who owns the risk, chooses to mitigate by naming a backup coordinator and writing a handover checklist. The one step still missing is the one that records what remains after the response. Which step should the owner take next?
choices: Reset the probability to its original high value so the register shows the starting point again.
Record the residual risk, meaning the risk left after the response, and update the register with it.
Transfer the risk to the sponsor by adding a contract penalty clause to the coordinator's role.
Convert the risk into an issue in the issue log, since the response has already been chosen.
questions.why: After a response is chosen, the owner records the residual risk, the amount of risk left over, in the register so the team can see how much exposure remains.

questions.prompt: Which statement best separates a risk from an issue in a project register?
choices: An issue is an uncertain future event that may affect the schedule, while a risk is a problem already under way.
A risk is an uncertain event that has not happened yet, while an issue is a risk that has already occurred and must be handled separately.
A risk is a problem that has already happened and needs an immediate fix, while an issue is a future possibility.
A risk and an issue are the same thing, recorded in different tools depending on the team's preference.
questions.why: A risk is uncertain because it has not happened, and once it happens it becomes an issue that is handled through a different process.

questions.prompt: A warehouse relocation team estimates there is a medium chance that a moving contractor will damage high-value equipment in transit. The team buys a policy from an insurer that pays for replacement if damage occurs. Which response does this purchase represent?
choices: Mitigate, because the purchase lowers the probability that the equipment is damaged.
Escalate, because the sponsor must make the decision to buy insurance for the move.
Transfer, because the financial consequence is shifted to the insurer through the policy.
Accept, because the team will simply watch the risk and do nothing else about it.
questions.why: Transfer shifts the consequence of the risk to another party, and an insurance policy that pays for replacement does exactly that without changing the chance of damage.

questions.prompt: A team's risk register contains one entry that reads: things could go wrong with the hardware vendor. There is no owner named, no probability or impact rating, and no response recorded. What is the main problem with this entry?
choices: The entry is recorded in the wrong file, since vendor risks belong in the issue log.
The entry has no score because vendor risks cannot be rated, so they should be removed from the register.
The vendor risk is too vague to act on, and without an owner, score or response nobody is positioned to watch or manage it.
The entry should be escalated to the sponsor immediately, because any vendor risk is automatically above the team's authority.
questions.why: A vague fear with no owner, score or response cannot be prioritised or watched, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns against.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that since the project has a risk register, risk management is done and the team can stop thinking about risk. Explain to them, in your own words, what a risk register is for, how one risk response differs from another, and one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would use for a risk you cannot afford to lose.
lessons.modelAnswer: A risk register is a living list of possible events that could affect the project, each with a score, an owner and a response. It is not finished when it is written; it is a tool for deciding where attention goes. The responses differ in what they change: avoid removes the cause, mitigate lowers the probability or impact but leaves some risk, transfer moves the financial or contractual burden to another party, and accept means we watch the risk and hold a contingency reserve. For a risk we truly cannot lose, such as a regulatory deadline, I would mitigate or avoid rather than accept, and escalate it to the sponsor if our reserve cannot cover it. The tradeoff is cost: each mitigation spends time or money now, so the team must judge whether the reduction is worth the spend. A register only helps if someone reviews it regularly.
rubricPoints: A risk is an uncertain future event, distinct from an issue that has already happened.
Risks are scored by probability and impact and recorded in a register with an owner.
Avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept and escalate each change the risk differently.
Every response has a cost or limit, and the register must be reviewed to stay useful.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers risk scoring and responses, and explaining the choice of response back to a teammate is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: An issue is a problem that is already happening on a project, not a worry about something that might happen later. Maybe a vendor delivered the wrong parts, or a key developer is off sick and testing has stalled. Issue management is the routine of writing each problem down in one shared list, giving it a named owner, judging how much it hurts the schedule, budget or quality, passing it up to the right person when needed, and tracking it until it is truly closed. Think of it as a shared to-do list for things that are broken right now.
lessons.guessPrompt: In a status meeting you learn that the shared test environment has been down for two days and nobody has written it down or been assigned to fix it. What is the most useful first step a project manager should take, and why?
lessons.teach:
An issue is a problem that exists right now and is affecting the project. The issue log is the single shared list where every open issue is recorded, with a description, an owner (the one named person responsible for getting it resolved), a priority, the date it was raised, and a status such as open, in progress, or closed. Escalation means passing an issue to a higher level of authority, such as a project sponsor or steering group, when the owner cannot resolve it with the time, people or budget they control. Resolution is the action that removes the problem, and closure happens only after someone checks that the fix actually worked.

Why it works: a problem written down with one owner and a target date cannot quietly drift. Everyone on the team can see what is blocked and who is chasing it.

Worked example: during testing, the shared test environment goes down. Step 1: log it as an issue the same day, describing the outage and its effect. Step 2: assign the infrastructure lead as owner. Step 3: estimate the impact, here testing is blocked and the release may slip three days. Step 4: the owner needs budget for an emergency vendor visit that they cannot approve, so escalate to the sponsor. Step 5: when the environment is back and the test suite passes, record the resolution, and close the issue only after the test lead confirms.

Common mistake: confusing an issue with a risk. A risk is an uncertain future event; an issue has already happened. A change request, a formal proposal to alter scope, schedule or budget, may be raised because of an issue, but it is tracked separately in change control.

Consequence: an issue with no owner and no log entry lives only in chat messages where nobody is accountable, so the schedule slips silently until the deadline is missed.

Issue management means logging, owning, escalating and closing problems that are already real.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union is preparing a core banking migration. During a rehearsal on Tuesday, the customer balance data feed fails to load. Step 1: the team logs it as an issue that day, describing the failed feed and its effect on the rehearsal. Step 2: the integration analyst, Priya Desai, is named as the single owner. Step 3: the impact is estimated. The rehearsal cannot finish, and the go-live date of 14 March may slip by about two days. Step 4: [missing]. Priya can approve overtime for her own team, but the vendor's emergency fee of 12,000 is beyond her authority. Step 5: once the feed reloads and the reconciliation totals match, the test lead confirms the fix and the issue is closed.
choices: Keep the issue with Priya and wait for the vendor to respond on its own schedule, since the owner is responsible for the outcome.
Raise a change request to move the go-live date and close the issue immediately, since the schedule has already changed.
Reclassify the failed feed as a risk so it is tracked in the risk register rather than the issue log.
Escalate the issue to the project sponsor, because the owner cannot fund the fee with the authority she holds.
questions.why: Escalation passes an issue to a higher level of authority when the owner cannot resolve it with the budget or people she controls, which is exactly the gap described in Step 4.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an issue rather than a risk?
choices: Leadership may decide to cut the testing budget in the next financial year.
A vendor warns that a future software update might break the interface, with a rough chance of 20 percent.
The payments server crashed at 9 a.m. and testing has stopped until it is restored.
The team suspects that a key contractor may leave the project next quarter.
questions.why: An issue is a problem that has already happened and is affecting the project now, whereas the other three describe uncertain future events, which are risks.

questions.prompt: A developer fixed a reporting bug on Monday and marked the issue closed the same afternoon, without the test lead checking the fix. Which statement best describes what went wrong?
choices: The issue should have been converted into a change request before the fix was applied.
The issue was closed too early, because closure happens only after someone checks that the fix actually worked.
Nothing went wrong, because closing an issue is the owner's decision once the code has been changed.
The issue should have stayed open until the sponsor signed off, because closure always needs executive approval.
questions.why: Closure is only valid after a check confirms the resolution worked, so closing on the developer's word alone skips that verification.

questions.prompt: On a warehouse system project, an issue was logged with a clear description and priority, but no single person was named to resolve it. The team agreed that everyone would look into it together. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The issue is automatically escalated to the sponsor once the priority is marked high.
The issue lives in chat messages where nobody is accountable, and the schedule may slip silently until the deadline is missed.
The issue becomes a risk, because unowned problems are by definition uncertain.
The issue is resolved faster, because several people are working on it at once.
questions.why: The owner is the one named person accountable for resolution, and without one, the problem drifts unnoticed, so the schedule slips without anyone being responsible for it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an issue differs from a risk, and what goes wrong when an issue has no owner. Name one limit or tradeoff a project manager faces when deciding whether to escalate an issue.
lessons.modelAnswer: An issue is something that has already happened and is hurting the project now, like a test environment that has been down for two days. A risk is something that might happen later, like a vendor who may miss a delivery date. That difference matters because issues need action today, while risks need a plan in case they occur. When an issue has no owner, it sits in chat messages and nobody is accountable for fixing it, so the schedule slips without anyone noticing until the deadline is missed. The main tradeoff when escalating is timing: escalate too early and you burden the sponsor with problems the owner could fix alone; escalate too late and the delay has already spread to other work. A good project manager escalates when the owner lacks the authority, budget or people to resolve it within an agreed timeframe.
rubricPoints: Defines an issue as a problem that has already occurred, distinct from a risk that is still uncertain
Explains that an unowned issue is not tracked or resolved and causes silent schedule slippage
Names escalation as passing the issue to someone with more authority, budget or people
Gives a tradeoff or limit of escalation, such as escalating too early or too late

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario where the learner must sort a problem as an issue, a risk or a change request and choose the next step adds the most beyond reading the definitions.

lessons.plain: Schedule management is the job of planning when each piece of project work happens, how long it takes, and which pieces must wait for others. Think of renovating a kitchen: the tiler cannot start until the floor is level, and the painter cannot start until the walls are dry. Schedule management turns a list of tasks into a timeline the team can follow, shows which delays would actually push back the finish date, and gives you a fixed reference to measure progress against. It is not about working faster. It is about seeing the order and the chain of dependencies clearly before the work starts.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two tasks can run at the same time. A third task must wait until both of them are finished. The two tasks take 3 days and 6 days. How long must the team wait before the third task can start, and why?
lessons.teach:
A schedule is built from activities, the discrete pieces of work the team will do, each with an estimated duration, meaning the time it needs to complete. Schedule management is the process of defining those activities, putting them in order, estimating their durations, and setting a baseline, which is the approved version of the timeline you measure progress against. Order is recorded as dependencies. A predecessor is an activity that must happen before another activity, called its successor. The most common dependency is finish-to-start, where the successor cannot begin until the predecessor ends.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities from the start of the project to the finish. Its total length is the shortest possible project duration. Float, sometimes called slack, is how long an activity can slip without delaying the finish date. Activities on the critical path have zero float.

Worked example. Task A takes 3 days. Tasks B (2 days) and C (4 days) both depend on A finishing. Task D (1 day) depends on both B and C. Trace the paths. A, B, D totals 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 days. A, C, D totals 3 + 4 + 1 = 8 days. The longest path, A, C, D, is the critical path, so the project takes 8 days. Task B has 2 days of float: it could slip by two days and still not delay D.

Common mistake: adding every task's duration into one line, which gives 10 days here and ignores that B and C run side by side. Another mistake is spending effort to speed up a task that has float, which changes nothing about the finish date.

In practice, a slip on the critical path moves the finish date directly, while a slip within float does not, so that is where a project manager watches most closely.

questions.prompt: A small bakery is launching an online ordering page. Activities: Design the page (4 days). Write the menu content (6 days) and set up the payment account (2 days) both start only after the design is finished. Testing the page (3 days) starts only after both the menu content and the payment setup are finished. Trace the paths: Design, Menu, Testing totals 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 days. Design, Payment, Testing totals 4 + 2 + 3 = 9 days. The longest path, Design, Menu, Testing, is the critical path, so the launch takes 13 days. Question: how many days of float does the payment setup activity have?
choices: 4 days
9 days
0 days
2 days
questions.why: Float is the critical path length minus the length of the path through the activity, so 13 minus 9 gives 4 days of slack for the payment setup.

questions.prompt: In a finish-to-start dependency between a predecessor and a successor, which statement is correct?
choices: The predecessor must wait until the successor finishes before it can end
The successor may begin as soon as the predecessor is half complete
The successor must start at the same moment the predecessor starts
The successor cannot begin until the predecessor ends
questions.why: Finish-to-start means the successor is blocked until its predecessor is complete, which is the rule stated in the definition of this dependency type.

questions.prompt: A team has three activities: Survey (3 days), Order equipment (5 days, starts after the survey), and Train staff (2 days, starts after the survey). Install (4 days) starts after both the equipment order and the staff training finish. What is the shortest possible total duration of this project?
choices: 10 days
14 days
12 days
9 days
questions.why: The longest chain is Survey, Order, Install at 3 + 5 + 4 = 12 days, and the critical path sets the shortest possible project duration; adding all tasks together (14) ignores that Order and Train run side by side.

questions.prompt: A project has a permit approval task of 6 days that sits on a path with 3 days of float. The team pays for extra staff to cut the permit approval to 2 days, but the task still finishes before the critical path does. What happens to the project finish date?
choices: The finish date moves earlier by 4 days
No change, because the task had float and was not on the critical path
The finish date moves later by 3 days
The float on the critical path grows by 4 days
questions.why: Shortening a task that has float does not shorten the critical path, so the finish date stays the same and the extra spending gains nothing for the deadline.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a project schedule needs a critical path, and name one limit of relying on the critical path estimates.
lessons.modelAnswer: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, and it sets the shortest possible finish date for the project. We need it because tasks that run side by side do not add up; only the longest dependent chain decides when we can finish. Tasks on that path have zero float, so any slip there moves the end date, while tasks with float can absorb some delay. The limit is that the critical path is only as good as the duration estimates and dependencies we entered. If an estimate is optimistic or a dependency is missing, the real critical path can be a different chain, so we should re-check it whenever the work or the estimates change.
rubricPoints: Defines the critical path as the longest chain of dependent activities that sets the shortest finish date
Explains that float or slack shows how much a non-critical task can slip without delaying the end
States that critical path results depend on accurate durations and complete dependencies
Notes that the critical path can change when estimates or sequencing change

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises project scheduling, so this objective is best learned by reading the definitions and working one timeline by hand.

lessons.plain: Quality and performance management means making sure a project delivers something that works as promised, and checking along the way that the work is on track to do so. Quality means the finished thing meets agreed standards. Performance means how well the work is going compared with the plan, in time, money and output. Think of a head chef who tastes each dish before it leaves the kitchen, which checks quality, and who also watches how many orders go out on time, which checks performance. The team agrees up front what good looks like, measures against it regularly, and fixes gaps early instead of at handover.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team building a billing feature finishes the code on schedule and under budget, but customers report wrong totals on their invoices. Was the project successful? What would you have measured to catch the problem earlier?
lessons.teach: Quality planning means deciding before work starts what good means for each deliverable and how it will be checked. The measurable conditions a deliverable must meet are called acceptance criteria. Quality assurance (QA) checks the process that produces the work, for example peer reviews, standards audits and a test strategy, so defects are prevented. Quality control (QC) inspects the actual output against the acceptance criteria, for example running tests on a release or sampling invoices. Performance measurement compares what has happened with what was planned, using numbers. A common tool is earned value. Planned value (PV) is the budgeted cost of work scheduled to be done by now. Earned value (EV) is the budgeted cost of work actually completed. Actual cost (AC) is what was really spent. Schedule performance index (SPI) equals EV divided by PV; below 1 means behind schedule. Cost performance index (CPI) equals EV divided by AC; below 1 means over budget. Worked example: a migration project has PV of 20,000 credits and EV of 16,000 credits at a checkpoint, and AC is 20,000. Step one: SPI = 16,000 divided by 20,000 = 0.8, so the team is behind schedule. Step two: CPI = 16,000 divided by 20,000 = 0.8, so each credit spent has returned 0.8 credits of completed work. Step three: both signals point to a problem to investigate, not to a known cause. Common mistake: treating on-time, on-budget status as proof of quality. A deliverable can be finished early and cheap yet still fail its acceptance criteria. Metrics measure progress; QC measures whether the output is right. Consequence in a running system: a release that passed a schedule check but skipped QC can ship a defect that causes a live incident after go-live, when the fix costs far more than it would have during testing. Quality is judged against agreed criteria, not against the calendar.

questions.prompt: A city library team is building a booking portal. At a checkpoint, PV is 12,000 hours' worth of budgeted cost, EV is 15,000 and AC is 18,000. Step one: SPI = EV / PV = 15,000 / 12,000 = 1.25, so the team is ahead of schedule. Step two is missing. Which option completes step two correctly?
choices: CPI = 18,000 / 15,000 = 1.2, so the team is under budget.
CPI = 12,000 / 18,000 = 0.67, so the team is over budget.
CPI = 15,000 / 18,000 = 0.83, so the team is over budget.
CPI = 15,000 / 12,000 = 1.25, so the team is under budget.
questions.why: CPI is EV divided by AC, which gives 15,000 / 18,000, about 0.83, and a value below 1 means the team is over budget.

questions.prompt: A county permit-software team holds a weekly walkthrough of its coding standards and checks that a second developer reviews every change before it is merged. Which activity is this?
choices: Quality assurance, because it checks the process that produces the work
Acceptance testing, because it confirms the customer's criteria are met
Performance measurement, because it compares actual progress with the plan
Quality control, because it inspects finished output
questions.why: Quality assurance examines the process so that defects are prevented, while quality control inspects the output itself.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's status dashboard shows PV of 50,000, EV of 40,000 and AC of 36,000 for a warehouse-routing project. Which statement describes the project's position?
choices: On schedule and on budget, because the numbers are close to each other
Behind schedule and over budget, because EV is below both PV and AC
Behind schedule and under budget, because SPI is 0.8 and CPI is about 1.11
Ahead of schedule and over budget, because AC is below PV
questions.why: SPI is 40,000 / 50,000 = 0.8 (behind schedule) and CPI is 40,000 / 36,000, about 1.11 (under budget).

questions.prompt: A team reports that its sensor firmware release has an SPI of 1.1 and a CPI of 1.05, and concludes that the release is quality-approved. What is the main flaw in this conclusion?
choices: A CPI above 1 is only meaningful if actual cost was recorded in hours rather than credits.
A value of 1.05 is too close to 1 to count, so the team should wait until CPI reaches 2.0.
Any SPI above 1 proves the release is defect-free, so the conclusion is valid.
The indices measure schedule and cost, so they cannot show the firmware meets the agreed acceptance criteria; quality control testing is still needed.
questions.why: Performance indices report schedule and cost progress, and only inspection against acceptance criteria shows whether the output is right.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between quality assurance and quality control, and name one limit of using earned value numbers alone to judge a project's quality.
lessons.modelAnswer: Quality assurance checks the process that produces the work, such as reviews, audits and the test approach, so that defects are less likely to happen. Quality control checks the actual output against the agreed acceptance criteria, such as running tests on a release or sampling records. Earned value gives a view of schedule and cost, with SPI and CPI showing whether work is behind or over budget. Its limit is that it measures progress and spending, not correctness. A project can show good SPI and CPI while the delivered features fail acceptance tests. So I would pair the earned value numbers with QC results before saying the project is performing well.
rubricPoints: QA focuses on the process and preventing defects.
QC inspects the deliverable against acceptance criteria.
Earned value (SPI, CPI) measures schedule and cost progress.
Earned value does not prove the output is correct, so it must be paired with quality checks.

suggested.rationale: Telling a schedule-and-cost report apart from a real quality check is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style situation where both signals conflict.

lessons.plain: Communication management means deciding who on a project needs to know what, how often, through which channel, and in what form, so the right information reaches the right people without flooding them. Think of a relay race: the baton passes cleanly only when everyone knows when to run and where the handoff happens. Project managers write this down in a communication plan, then keep it current as people join, leave, or change their minds. It is less about sending lots of messages and more about making sure the messages that matter arrive, get understood, and lead to action.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project has three teams in three time zones. The sponsor asks for a status update every Friday, but the developers say weekly meetings keep pulling them away from their work. What would you do first so the sponsor gets accurate information without interrupting the developers every week?
lessons.teach:
Communication management is the part of project management that plans how project information is gathered, stored, distributed, and understood. Its main artifact is the communication plan, a document listing each stakeholder group (anyone with an interest in or influence over the project), the information that group needs, how often they need it, the format, the channel, and who is responsible for sending it. A sponsor is the person who funds and is accountable for the project. An operator is someone who runs the result after delivery.

It works because different audiences need different detail. A sponsor needs a short view of schedule, budget, and risk. A delivery team needs task-level detail and blockers. Writing these needs down prevents both silence and overload.

Worked example: a team is migrating a fleet-tracking service. Step one, list stakeholders: sponsor, operations on-call, customer support, developers. Step two, record each group's needs. The sponsor gets a one-page summary by email every Friday, owned by the project manager. Operations gets a shared change calendar and an escalation channel for outages. Support gets a short note before each customer-visible change. Step three, agree the plan with stakeholders, then review it at each milestone and update it when needs change.

Common mistake: treating communication as sending the same weekly email to everyone and assuming it was received and understood. Sending is not the same as being understood. Confirm key messages, such as a moved release date, with the people who must act on them.

If the on-call team never learns that the migration window has moved, they may page a supposedly stable system during a live cutover, turning a planned change into an incident. Communication management means making the plan deliberate, matched to each audience, and checked for whether it actually worked.

questions.prompt: A regional library network is replacing its book-loan system. Its project manager is writing a communication plan, where a communication plan is the document that lists each stakeholder group (anyone with an interest in or influence over the project), what that group needs to know, how often, in what format, through which channel, and who sends it. Steps one and two are done. Step one, list stakeholders: the funding board, branch staff, the help desk, and library patrons' representative committee. Step two, record needs: the funding board gets a one-page summary by email every two weeks, owned by the project manager; branch staff get a shared calendar of system downtime and a direct line to the help desk; the help desk gets a short note 48 hours before each change that affects logins; the patrons' committee gets a notice before any change to borrowing limits. Step three is missing from the plan. Which step completes the plan as described?
choices: Agree the plan with each stakeholder group, then review it at each milestone and update it when their needs change.
Send the same full technical release notes to all four groups and treat the plan as finished.
Share the plan only with the IT staff who build the system, since they are the ones who need it most.
Have the project manager choose the channel for the funding board without asking the board.
questions.why: Step three in this process is to agree the plan with stakeholders and then review and update it, which is the step that checks whether the plan actually works for each audience.

questions.prompt: In a communication plan, what is recorded for each stakeholder group?
choices: The information the group needs, how often, the format, the channel, and who is responsible for sending it.
A list of every task that group's members must complete this week.
Only the project budget and the schedule for that group.
The vendor contract terms that group is allowed to read.
questions.why: A communication plan records, per stakeholder group, the information needed, frequency, format, channel, and the responsible sender, which is the full set described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A warehouse automation project has a sponsor (the person who funds the project and is accountable for it). A project manager must decide what the sponsor should receive. Which choice best fits the sponsor's needs?
choices: A short summary covering schedule, budget, and risk, sent on a regular rhythm.
No update, since the sponsor is only interested once the system goes live.
A full copy of the test scripts so the sponsor can check each case.
A daily log of every blocker raised by each developer on the team.
questions.why: A sponsor needs a short view of schedule, budget, and risk, so a brief regular summary is the matching format, while task-level detail belongs to the delivery team.

questions.prompt: A hospital's scheduling team sent one email to all staff announcing that a system cutover moved to a later date. Weeks later, nurses still booked appointments on the old system. Which step would most likely have prevented this gap?
choices: Confirming the moved date with the nurses and schedulers who had to act on it, rather than assuming the email was understood.
Removing the schedulers from the list because they are not sponsors.
Sending the email again to all staff in a larger font.
Waiting until the cutover date to announce the change so nobody is confused early.
questions.why: Sending a message does not guarantee it was understood, so confirming key messages with the people who must act on them is the check that would have exposed the gap.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the project what communication management covers, and name one tradeoff a project manager must balance when deciding how often and how much to communicate.
lessons.modelAnswer: Communication management covers planning how project information is gathered, distributed, and understood, usually written down in a communication plan. The plan names each stakeholder group, what they need to know, how often, through which channel, and who sends it. The tradeoff is frequency and detail against overload. Communicating too rarely leaves people surprised or acting on stale information, while communicating too often or in too much detail wastes time and trains people to ignore messages, including the urgent ones. A good manager tailors each message to its audience, uses a short summary for sponsors and detail for doers, and checks that key messages were actually understood, not just sent.
rubricPoints: Defines communication management as planning how project information is distributed and understood
Mentions the communication plan and stakeholder needs, frequency, channel, and owner
Names a real tradeoff such as too little communication versus information overload
Notes that sending a message does not guarantee it was received and understood

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises stakeholder communication planning, so being able to explain the plan and its tradeoffs back is the core skill.

lessons.plain: Meeting management is the practice of planning, running and following up on the meetings a project depends on, so that people spend their time on decisions rather than talk. A project manager decides who needs to be in the room, what each meeting is for, what it must decide, and who does what afterward. Think of it like a shared kitchen timer and a notebook: time is limited, and what gets written down is what the team can act on later. The skill is less about being a good talker and more about making sure every meeting ends with clear outcomes.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your project team has met for an hour every Monday for a month, and the schedule has not moved. What is the most likely reason, and what single change to how the meetings are run would you try first?
lessons.teach:
A meeting type is the purpose a meeting serves. A kickoff starts work and sets expectations. A status meeting checks progress against plan. A steering meeting is where sponsors, the people who fund and authorize the project, make decisions about budget or scope. A retrospective is a review where the team looks back at a finished period and considers what to change. Each type needs a different length, audience and output. An agenda is the ordered list of topics with a time allowance for each, shared before the meeting. Timeboxing means giving each topic a fixed slot and moving on when it runs out. A facilitator keeps the discussion on track. A note-taker records outcomes. Minutes are the written record of what was discussed and decided. A decision log is a running list of decisions with the date and who made them. An action item is a task with one named owner and a due date.

Why it works: a meeting produces value only when it changes something afterward. Writing down decisions and owners turns talk into commitments that can be checked at the next meeting. A shared agenda lets people prepare, so the meeting time is spent deciding rather than catching up.

Worked example: a status meeting is set for 60 minutes with five topics. The project manager sends the agenda the day before: budget (10 minutes), vendor delay (15), test plan (15), staffing (10), next steps (10). The facilitator opens with the vendor delay. The discussion runs 25 minutes, so the facilitator says the group will take the vendor decision offline, and the note-taker logs it as an open item. The test plan review finishes on time. Within a day the minutes go out with three action items, each with one owner and a date.

Common mistake: holding a meeting with no agenda and no recorded decisions, so the same question returns the following week. In a running project, the consequence is that the vendor delay gets discussed in three meetings, nobody owns the fix, and the schedule slips without anyone noticing.

Meeting management ensures that every meeting ends with a recorded decision or a named owner for each follow-up.

questions.prompt: A county library runs a steering meeting to decide on a project change. The sponsor, who funds the project, approves adding barcode scanners to the scope, and the note-taker writes this in the decision log: 'Barcode scanners added to scope, 14 March.' One required element is still missing from this log entry. What should be added to complete it?
choices: The name of the sponsor who made the decision
A list of every team member who attended the meeting
The facilitator's name, since the facilitator ran the discussion
The name of the vendor who will supply the scanners
questions.why: A decision log entry must record the date and who made the decision, and the sponsor who approved the scope change is the decision maker, so their name completes the entry.

questions.prompt: A product team finishes a two-week working period and gathers to look back at what went well, what did not, and what to change next time. Which meeting type is this?
choices: Retrospective
Status meeting
Kickoff
Steering meeting
questions.why: A retrospective is the review where the team looks back at a finished period and considers what to change, which matches this gathering.

questions.prompt: A 30-minute meeting has four agenda topics, each allotted 7 minutes. The first topic runs 14 minutes and the group is still debating it when its slot ends. Which action best follows the timeboxing approach described for meetings?
choices: Let the first topic run until it is settled, and drop the last topic
Keep discussing the first topic and extend the meeting by 14 minutes
Start the second topic early to save time for the rest of the agenda
Stop at the 7-minute mark, record the unresolved point as an open item, and move on
questions.why: Timeboxing means giving each topic a fixed slot and moving on when it runs out, with unfinished points recorded so they can be followed up rather than letting one topic consume the meeting.

questions.prompt: At the end of a team meeting, someone says, 'We should look into the server reliability issues.' Nobody is named and no date is set, and the meeting closes. Which element of meeting management is missing, and what is the consequence in a running project?
choices: The meeting is missing a steering sponsor, so the budget decision cannot be made
The meeting has too many topics, so the facilitator should have timeboxed the discussion more strictly
The follow-up is an action item without one named owner or a due date, so the task is likely to be discussed again without anyone fixing it
The minutes are missing a copy of the agenda, so the team cannot prepare for next time
questions.why: An action item must have one named owner and a due date, and without them the follow-up is not a commitment, so the issue tends to return in later meetings while nobody works on it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just been asked to run the weekly project status meeting how to structure it so it produces decisions, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would run it with a short written agenda sent a day ahead, with each topic timeboxed. Someone other than the person leading takes notes, so the facilitator can keep the discussion moving. Every item should end in one of three outcomes: a decision recorded in the decision log, an action item with one owner and a due date, or an open issue parked for a separate session. Minutes go out within a day. The tradeoff is that a tight timebox can cut off a real problem before it is understood. If a topic overruns, I would not stretch the meeting. I would schedule a focused follow-up with only the people who need to decide, so the rest of the team is not pulled into a conversation they do not need.
rubricPoints: Names an agenda shared before the meeting, with timeboxed topics
Separates the facilitator role from the note-taker role
Requires each item to end in a recorded decision, an owned action item, or a parked issue
Names a real limit, such as a timebox cutting off an unfinished problem, and a way to handle it

suggested.rationale: Explaining how to run a meeting back to a teammate, including its limits, is the core skill here and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: Team and resource management is about making sure the right people, skills, equipment and money are available to do the project's work, at the right time, without overloading anyone. Think of a kitchen during a dinner rush: the cooks, ovens and ingredients all have limits, so the head chef decides who works on what and when. A project manager does the same with people and other shared assets, watching who is free, who is overbooked, and who has the skills a task needs. The goal is a team that can actually deliver, not just a list of names on a plan.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project plan shows one engineer assigned to three tasks that all start in the same week, and each task alone would take her full week. Before any teaching, what do you think will happen to the schedule, and what would you do about it?
lessons.teach:
A resource is anything the project consumes to do its work: people, specialist skills, test environments, licences, equipment, or budget. Resource management is the planning and control of those resources. Resource allocation means assigning a specific resource to a specific task. Over-allocation means one person is booked for more hours than they have available, and it is one of the most common hidden causes of slipped dates. Float, sometimes called slack, is how much a task can be delayed without moving the project's end date.

Resource leveling is a fix for over-allocation. You move or stretch tasks so that no one exceeds their available hours, usually accepting a longer schedule in exchange for a realistic one. Resource smoothing is a related technique that shifts work only within the float each task already has, so the finish date does not move, though some overload may remain. Choosing between them is a tradeoff: leveling protects the team but can lengthen the schedule.

Team management also covers roles. A RACI chart lists, for each deliverable, who is Responsible for doing the work, who is Accountable for it being done (only one person), who must be Consulted, and who must be Informed.

Worked example: Priya has 40 available hours a week. She is assigned a design review of 30 hours and an API build of 30 hours, both in week one, so she is booked for 60 hours, or 150 percent. Step 1: spot the overload on the resource view. Step 2: check float; the design review has a week of slack before it blocks the release. Step 3: move the review into week two. Step 4: Priya now carries 30 hours in each week, and the finish date holds.

Common mistake: assuming that a name listed on a task means that person is available for it. Availability depends on other work, leave and skill fit.

Consequence: if over-allocation is not caught, the schedule looks correct on paper and then slips by weeks when the work collides in practice.

questions.prompt: Omar has 30 available hours a week. In week one he is booked for UAT coordination (18 hours) and cutover rehearsal (16 hours), 34 hours in total, which is 113 percent of his capacity. Step 1: the resource view shows the overload in week one. Step 2: check float. UAT coordination has three days of float, meaning it can be delayed that long without moving the project end date. The cutover rehearsal has no float because it blocks the release. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the finish date holds, and a 4-hour overload remains in week one.
choices: Move the cutover rehearsal into week two, which lengthens the schedule by a week.
Delete the UAT coordination from the plan so that week one is no longer overloaded.
Leave both tasks in week one, since 113 percent is a small overload and the schedule looks correct on paper.
Shift part of the UAT coordination into its three days of float, so the finish date holds even though some overload may remain.
questions.why: Resource smoothing shifts work only within each task's existing float, so the end date holds and some overload may remain, which is exactly what the missing step and the stated result describe.

questions.prompt: Ines, a data analyst, has a reporting task with four days of float. Her manager asks how far the task can slip before the project end date moves. Which answer is correct?
choices: Four days, since float is how far a task can be delayed without moving the project end date.
Zero, since any delay to a non-critical task moves the finish date.
Four days, but only if Ines has no other work booked that week.
Eight days, because float adds the slip allowed for the task to the slip allowed for its predecessor.
questions.why: Float is defined as how much a task can be delayed without moving the project's end date, so the answer is the four days of float, not conditions on other work or added totals.

questions.prompt: On a new mobile login feature, Tomas will write the code, Ayesha will approve the release, Kwame will also be marked Accountable for the release, and Ben must be consulted on security. Which assignment breaks the RACI rule?
choices: Ben is Consulted on the security aspects.
Ayesha and Kwame are both marked Accountable for the release.
Tomas is Responsible for writing the login code.
Priya is Informed when the release ships.
questions.why: A RACI chart allows only one person to be Accountable for each deliverable, so two Accountable names on the release is the breach, while the other three assignments use roles correctly.

questions.prompt: A vendor-facing launch date is fixed by contract. Sam's build task is over-allocated and has no float. Which response is correct?
choices: Apply smoothing, which moves work within float so the launch date holds.
Apply smoothing, which cannot shift zero-float work, so the overload stays, and leveling would push the fixed launch date out.
Ignore the overload, because over-allocation only matters on tasks that have float.
Apply leveling, since it never moves the finish date.
questions.why: Smoothing only shifts work within existing float, so with zero float it cannot help, and leveling fixes overload by lengthening the schedule, which conflicts with the fixed date.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between resource leveling and resource smoothing, and name the main tradeoff a project manager accepts when leveling a schedule.
lessons.modelAnswer: Resource leveling and resource smoothing both fix overloaded people, but they differ in what they protect. Leveling moves or stretches tasks until nobody exceeds their available hours, even if that changes the critical path, so the end date can move later. Smoothing only shifts work inside the float each task already has, so the finish date stays put, but it cannot always remove every overload. The tradeoff with leveling is schedule length: you buy a realistic team load by accepting a later finish, and stakeholders should hear about that before it happens. So I would level when the end date is flexible and smooth when the date is fixed, and I would say which one we used.
rubricPoints: Leveling resolves over-allocation by moving or stretching tasks until no one exceeds available hours.
Smoothing shifts work only within existing float, so the finish date is protected but some overload may remain.
Leveling usually lengthens the schedule, and that tradeoff must be communicated to stakeholders.
A strong answer chooses the technique based on whether the end date is fixed or flexible.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine teaches resource allocation, so explaining the leveling versus smoothing tradeoff back is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Procurement is the process of getting things from outside your organization, such as software licenses, hardware, cloud services, or consultants, when your project should not build them itself. Vendor selection is the step where you choose which outside supplier to use. It works like hiring a builder for a house extension: you describe what you need, ask several builders to quote, compare their prices and track records against what matters most to you, and then sign a written agreement that states what they will deliver and what happens if they fall short. Done well, it gets you the right supplier at a fair price with clear responsibilities. Done badly, it leaves you tied to someone who cannot deliver.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your project needs a reporting tool that your team has no time to build, and three vendors could supply one. What would you want to see from each before picking one, and why might the cheapest quote not be the best choice?
lessons.teach:
Procurement is acquiring goods or services from outside the project. Before buying, a make-or-buy analysis asks whether building in-house is cheaper, faster, or safer than buying. If buying, a request for information (RFI) asks vendors what they can offer, a request for proposal (RFP) asks for a detailed solution and price against your stated requirements, and a request for quote (RFQ) asks for a price on a fully defined item. A statement of work (SOW) describes exactly what the vendor must deliver. Selection is usually done with weighted scoring: each criterion, such as security, cost, support, or integration, gets a weight that adds up to 100 percent, and each vendor gets a score per criterion. Contract types decide who carries cost risk. In a fixed-price contract the vendor carries most of the risk, and the buyer knows the price up front but gets less flexibility. In a cost-reimbursable contract the buyer pays actual costs plus a fee, so the buyer carries the risk. Time and materials pays for hours at agreed rates, which suits uncertain work.

Worked example: a team needs a ticketing system for 200 users. Building it would tie up two developers for six months, so they choose to buy. They weight security 30 percent, cost 25 percent, support 25 percent, and integration 20 percent. Vendor A scores 4, 3, 5, and 3 out of 5, giving 1.2 + 0.75 + 1.25 + 0.6 = 3.80. Vendor B scores 3, 5, 3, and 4, giving 0.9 + 1.25 + 0.75 + 0.8 = 3.70. Vendor A wins despite the higher price, and the scores are recorded so the choice can be defended.

The common mistake is choosing on price alone, or writing a vague SOW. Vague requirements lead to disputed deliverables and change requests, and the schedule slips while both sides argue. In a running system this shows up as a vendor who technically meets the contract but fails the uptime the team needed, because no service level agreement (SLA) defined that target. Procurement is not finished at signature; the contract must be managed until the vendor's work is accepted and the contract is closed.

questions.prompt: A library is choosing a room-booking system using weighted scoring. The criteria are accessibility at 40 percent, price at 35 percent, and training at 25 percent, which together make 100 percent. Vendor X scores 4, 2, and 5 out of 5. Vendor Y scores 3, 5, and 3. Step 1: multiply each score by its weight written as a decimal, so Vendor X gets 1.6, 0.7, and 1.25. Step 2 is missing. Step 3: choose the vendor with the highest total. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: Add the weighted results for each vendor to get one total
Average the raw scores for each vendor, ignoring the weights
Multiply the two largest weighted results together
Divide each vendor's price score by the number of criteria
questions.why: Weighted scoring turns each vendor's per-criterion results into a single comparable total by adding the weighted results together, which is why the library can compare X and Y directly.

questions.prompt: A charity knows the exact specification of 50 identical laptops it needs and wants vendors to quote one unit price for that fully defined item. Which procurement document fits this purpose?
choices: A request for quote (RFQ)
A make-or-buy analysis
A request for information (RFI)
A request for proposal (RFP)
