Imagine a project that collects customers' home addresses. Before building anything, you need to know which rules cover that data, what they demand, and how you will prove you met them. For a project manager, this means putting those requirements into the plan, the design and the tests from the start, rather than discovering them at launch.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team is building an app that stores delivery drivers' GPS locations for a logistics company. Someone suggests keeping every location point forever in case it is useful later. What concerns would you raise, and why?
lessons.teach:
A requirement is a rule the project must satisfy. A compliance requirement comes from an outside source you are bound to, such as a law, a regulation, a contract or an industry standard. Compliance means meeting those requirements and being able to show evidence that you did. A privacy requirement is a subset focused on personal data, meaning any information that identifies a person or can reasonably be linked to one. Key privacy ideas include data minimization (collect only what the purpose needs), purpose limitation (use the data only for the stated reason), retention (keep data only as long as needed, then delete it) and access control (only the right people can see it). The data subject is the person the data is about. The data owner is the person accountable for a dataset inside the organization.

Why it works: rules about personal data limit harm. Each limit shrinks what can leak, be misused or be kept past its usefulness, and the evidence trail lets an auditor confirm the limits are real.

Worked example: a logistics firm wants driver GPS points for route planning. Step 1: identify the data as personal, because a location tied to a driver identifies that driver. Step 2: minimize, since route planning needs a position every few minutes, not every second indefinitely. Step 3: set retention, for example 30 days, then automated deletion. Step 4: restrict access to dispatch staff, with access logged. Step 5: record each decision so an audit can trace it.

Common mistake: treating compliance as a final review before launch. Requirements found late force redesign, and the team often cannot show when a control was added.

Consequence: if the deletion job is missing, the data store grows with personal records the policy says should be gone, and every backup copies them too. Compliance is a property of the running system, not just of the document.

questions.prompt: A regional hotel chain runs a guest loyalty app. Marketing wants to send birthday discounts, so the team plans to store each guest's full date of birth. Step 1: identify the date of birth as personal data, because it is tied to a specific guest. Step 2: minimize, since a birthday discount needs only the month and day, not the birth year. Step 3 is left blank for you to complete: it covers retention, meaning how long the birth data is kept before it is removed. Which option correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Share the birth dates with partner vendors so they can send their own birthday offers.
Delete the stored birth dates automatically 90 days after the guest closes the loyalty account.
Skip any record of this decision, because the purpose of birthday discounts is obvious to everyone on the team.
Keep the birth dates indefinitely so they are available if a guest asks for an offer years later.
questions.why: Retention means keeping personal data only as long as it is needed and then deleting it, and a set period after the account closes with automated deletion matches that rule.

questions.prompt: In the teaching text's terms, who is the data subject?
choices: The person accountable for a dataset inside the organization.
The auditor who checks whether the limits are real.
The person the data is about.
The engineer who writes the deletion job.
questions.why: The text defines the data subject as the person the data is about, while the data owner is the accountable person inside the organization.

questions.prompt: A team building a fitness app collects a heart-rate reading every second and keeps every reading forever, even though the feature only shows a daily resting-heart-rate average. Which change best applies data minimization?
choices: Keep readings for as long as the app stays installed, with no deletion date set.
Keep every second of readings for the life of the app so that future features have full history.
Collect only the daily resting-heart-rate average the feature needs and stop storing the raw readings.
Store all readings on a shared drive so every engineer can review them when needed.
questions.why: Data minimization means collecting only what the purpose needs, and a daily average is enough for a feature that shows only that average.

questions.prompt: A project team plans to add the deletion job for personal records after the first release, reasoning that the data set is small for now. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: An auditor automatically approves the system because the data set is small.
The personal data becomes anonymous by default, so no retention rule applies.
The store accumulates personal records past their useful life, and every backup copies them too.
Users are no longer able to log in, because the deletion job blocks authentication.
questions.why: Without the deletion job, personal records the policy says should be gone remain in the store and are copied into backups, which the teaching text names as the consequence.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would make sure a new project meets its privacy requirements, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing which rules apply: the privacy law where our users live, any contract with a customer, and our own company policy. Then I would ask what personal data the project truly needs and cut the rest, since less data means less risk. Each kind of data gets a stated purpose, a retention period and a named owner, and deletion becomes a task on the plan rather than a promise. We keep evidence such as access logs and signed-off decisions so an auditor can check them. The tradeoff is that minimizing data can make some features harder, such as analytics that want full history. We would need to agree that tradeoff with the business and, where we are unsure what a rule requires, get legal advice rather than guess.
rubricPoints: Identifies which rules apply, including laws, contracts and internal policy
Explains minimization, purpose limitation and retention as ways to reduce risk
Describes how requirements become tasks, controls and evidence in the plan
Names a real tradeoff, such as reduced analytics or feature cost, and who decides it

suggested.rationale: A scenario where the learner must decide which privacy controls apply fits this objective better than any listed mission, and none of the current missions covers compliance.

lessons.plain: IT concepts for project management are the basic building blocks of technology that projects are built from, such as servers, networks, databases, storage, and the software environments where work is tested before it goes live. You do not need to build these yourself, but you do need enough vocabulary to ask good questions, understand what a delivery will touch, and notice when a schedule or budget ignores a technical step. Think of it like renovating a house: you need to know where the pipes, wiring and load-bearing walls are, even if a specialist does the work.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team says their new feature works on a developer's laptop, but it still must be tested on a separate copy of the system before customers see it. Why would a project manager care whether that separate copy exists, and what could go wrong if it were skipped?
lessons.teach:
An IT environment is a complete set of servers, networks, storage and software arranged for one purpose. Most projects use several. A development environment is where engineers build, a test environment (often called staging) is where the finished change is checked, and a production environment is the live system that real users depend on. A server is a computer that provides a service to other computers. A network is the set of links that lets them communicate. An API (application programming interface) is an agreed set of requests one piece of software can send to another. A database stores the records a system relies on, and its structure is called a schema. On-premises means the organisation runs the equipment itself; cloud means a provider supplies that capacity on demand.

Why this matters: each layer has its own lead time, cost and failure modes, so the schedule and budget depend on them.

Worked example: a team adds card payments to an online shop. First, developers build the feature in the development environment. Second, they connect to the payment provider's API, which needs network access and credentials. Third, they change the database schema to store payment references. Fourth, they test in the staging environment using a copy of the data. Fifth, production receives the change, and the project manager has scheduled a window for the schema change, because it cannot be undone instantly.

Common mistake: assuming a passing test environment proves production will behave the same. Production may have more users, different network rules, or larger data, so tests can pass while the live system fails.

Consequence: if the environments differ and this is not planned for, the release fails at the last step, the go-live date slips, and the delay is often blamed on the schedule rather than the missing infrastructure.

The project manager's job is not to configure these layers but to know which ones a deliverable touches and to ask when each one will be ready.

questions.prompt: A school district runs its timetable system on servers in its own building and plans to move it to a cloud provider, which supplies computing capacity on demand. First, the team builds the new system in a development environment, where engineers build. Second, they set up a test environment, often called staging, where the finished change is checked, and copy the timetable database into it. Third, the test environment is found to allow about 10 simultaneous users, while the live production system must support about 2,000. Fourth, [missing step]. Fifth, production receives the move, and the project manager schedules a window for the cutover. What belongs in the missing fourth step?
choices: Declare the test passed since the database loaded.
Move the test environment back on-premises for fixed capacity.
Skip staging and go straight to production.
Ask the provider to match test capacity to production, then repeat the load test at about 2,000 users.
questions.why: The team must close the capacity gap between staging and production and retest at live scale, because a test that passes at 10 users does not prove production will hold 2,000.

questions.prompt: A project team says its new feature works in the development environment. Which environment should it be checked in next, before real users depend on it?
choices: The development environment again, since the code is already there.
The network links between servers, since they carry the traffic.
The live production system, since users are waiting for it.
The test environment, often called staging, where the finished change is checked.
questions.why: Staging is the environment where the finished change is checked before it reaches production, so it is the correct next stop after development.

questions.prompt: A booking app's payment connection works in test but fails in production because production's network rules block the payment provider's address. Which layer caused the failure?
choices: The database schema, which must have changed.
The API design, since the requests are identical in both places.
The network layer, since production rules differ from the test environment.
The developers' work in the development environment.
questions.why: The API and schema are the same in both places, so the difference is in the network rules, a known way that environments diverge and tests can pass while production fails.

questions.prompt: A project manager is told a change will add a new column to a live customer database table. Why should the change be scheduled into a window rather than applied at any time?
choices: Users cannot log in during any database change at all.
The schema change cannot be undone instantly, so it needs a planned time.
The test environment must receive the change first before anything else happens.
The new column needs disk space that only frees up at set times.
questions.why: A schema change cannot be reversed instantly, so the project manager schedules it into a planned window to manage the risk to the running system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked in IT what the difference between development, test and production environments is, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on the test environment before a release.
lessons.modelAnswer: Development is where engineers build and experiment, so it can be messy and may hold fake data. Test, often called staging, is a copy of the system set up to resemble production, where the finished change is checked before anyone relies on it. Production is the live system that real customers and staff use, so changes there need care. The main limit of testing is that a test environment is never perfectly identical to production. It usually has less traffic, fewer users, smaller data volumes and sometimes different network or security settings. A release can pass every test and still fail under real load or with real data, so the team plans a gradual rollout or a rollback path rather than treating the test result as a guarantee.
rubricPoints: Defines development, test or staging, and production environments by their purpose.
Explains that environments differ in data, load, or settings from production.
Names a tradeoff, such as the cost of keeping a close match to production or the limits of test results.
Connects environment readiness to schedule or budget risk.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly shared vocabulary and how the layers relate, so reading the teaching text and then checking understanding by explaining it fits best.

lessons.plain: IT change control is the agreed process for deciding, testing, approving, and recording any change to a live computer system or software, such as a code release, a server setting, or a database update. Think of it as a checkpoint: before anyone touches a system that people depend on, the proposed change is written down, its risks are weighed by people who did not make it, and a plan exists for undoing it if things go wrong. Project managers rely on it because one unplanned edit can break services many people use at once, and the record it leaves shows everyone what changed and when.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer wants to change a database setting on the live production system tonight to fix a slow page. What should happen before they make that change, and who should know about it? Explain your reasoning in a few sentences.
lessons.teach:
A change request is a written proposal that states what will change, why, who is affected, and how risky it is. A change advisory board, usually shortened to CAB, is the group that reviews these requests and approves or rejects them; it normally includes people from operations, security, and the business, not only the person who wants the change. A baseline is the approved, known state of a system, such as a specific software version and configuration, against which later changes are compared. A rollback plan is the documented way to return to the baseline if a change fails. A standard change is pre-approved and low risk, so it follows a known routine without a fresh review. An emergency change skips the normal wait for urgent fixes but still gets a record and an after-the-fact review. The process works because a change that is written down, tested, and reversible can be judged by people who did not make it, which catches mistakes before users see them.

Worked example: a team plans to upgrade a payments library from version 2.4 to 2.5. Step 1: the developer files a change request describing the upgrade, the reason (a security fix), and the risk. Step 2: impact analysis finds that three services call the library. Step 3: the upgrade runs in a test environment, where one call fails and is fixed. Step 4: the CAB approves it for the Tuesday 22:00 change window. Step 5: the rollback plan keeps the 2.4 build ready and lists the steps to restore it. Step 6: after deployment, the team checks the results and closes the record.

Common mistake: treating a small edit as too minor to record. A one-line configuration change made directly on a live server leaves no trace, so when errors start the next day, nobody knows what changed.

In a running system, unrecorded changes slow incident diagnosis and turn a safe rollback into guesswork. The change process is what lets a team say exactly which version is live and return to a known good state within minutes.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union's mobile banking team wants to shorten the idle session timeout from 10 minutes to 5 minutes, a change driven by an internal security policy. The team has completed these steps: Step 1, a written change request states the change, the policy reason, and the users affected. Step 2, impact analysis finds that the login service and the mobile API both read this timeout value. Step 3, the change advisory board (CAB, the group that reviews and approves changes) approves the change for the Thursday 23:00 window. Step 4 is missing. Step 5, the change is deployed. Step 6, the team checks results and closes the record. Which item belongs at Step 4, before deployment?
choices: Document a rollback plan that keeps the 10-minute timeout configuration ready and lists the steps to restore it.
Ask the CAB to reclassify the change as an emergency change so it skips the window.
Skip any further record, because the change is only a single configuration value.
Deploy to production first and run the staging tests afterward to save time.
questions.why: A rollback plan written before deployment is the documented way to return the system to its approved baseline if the change fails, and it has to exist before the change goes live.

questions.prompt: In IT change control, what is a baseline?
choices: The list of people who must sign off on every change request before it can be scheduled.
The approved, known state of a system, such as a specific software version and configuration, against which later changes are compared.
A copy of a live database that is kept off-site in case of a disaster.
The time window each month when the team is allowed to deploy non-urgent updates.
questions.why: A baseline is defined as the approved, known state of a system that later changes are measured against, so the choice describing it as that known state is correct.

questions.prompt: A university IT team renews the TLS certificate on its public web servers every quarter. They use a script that operations has already reviewed, and the steps never change. Which change category best fits this renewal?
choices: No change record is needed, because the renewal does not alter any application code.
Standard change, because it is pre-approved, low risk, and follows a known routine without a fresh review.
Change request with full CAB review at every quarter, because any change to a live server needs a fresh review.
Emergency change, because certificate renewals always need to happen immediately.
questions.why: A standard change is pre-approved, low risk, and follows a known routine, which matches a quarterly renewal run by a reviewed script.

questions.prompt: A retailer applies a database schema update during its Friday evening peak. The team has no documented rollback plan and no recorded baseline of the schema before the update. The update corrupts some order records, and the team cannot return the database to its prior state. What is the most direct gap in the change process?
choices: The after-deployment review was held too late to catch the corruption.
The change was not approved by a large enough group of people.
There was no approved baseline and documented rollback path to return the system to a known good state.
The update should have been filed as an emergency change to speed up approval.
questions.why: Without a recorded baseline and a documented rollback path, the team has no known good state to return to, which is the direct gap that left them unable to recover.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a software release why IT change control exists and what it costs the team in time. Name one real limit or tradeoff of this process.
lessons.modelAnswer: Change control exists because a live system is fragile and many people depend on it, so every change should be written down, checked by someone other than the author, and reversible. The cost is time: a change request, impact analysis, and a CAB review can delay a fix by days, and a team under pressure may be tempted to skip the process. That tradeoff is real. The safeguard is to match the process to the risk, using standard changes for routine low-risk work and emergency changes for urgent fixes, while still recording them afterward. Without a record, nobody can tell which version is live or undo a bad change quickly.
rubricPoints: Change control means recording, reviewing, and approving changes to live systems before they happen
A rollback plan or baseline lets the team return to a known good state if the change fails
Review by people other than the author catches risks the author may miss
The process costs time, and it can tempt teams to skip it under pressure
Matching the process to risk, with standard, normal, and emergency paths, is the usual way to balance this

suggested.rationale: A realistic release scenario where the learner must decide what review, testing, and rollback steps apply adds the most to this change-control objective.

scenarios.title: Scanner Rollout at Harbor Lantern Logistics
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional company that runs three regional warehouses. Dana, a new project manager, is leading a project to replace paper stock counts with a barcode tracking system. The project has two parts. The first is installing handheld barcode scanners, which must meet a fixed regulatory standard and a fixed delivery date. The second is building the tracking software, which the team develops in two-week iterations called sprints, where a small set of features is designed, built, and tested before the next set begins. Dana must decide how to manage each part. Partway through, the warehouse operations lead asks for a live stock dashboard to be added to the current sprint. At the same time, the scanner vendor warns that a shipment may arrive three weeks late. Answer the following:
1. Recommend waterfall or agile for each of the two parts of the project, where waterfall means completing one phase fully before starting the next, and agile means delivering work in short repeating cycles with feedback. Give one reason for each recommendation.
2. Describe the change-control step Dana should take with the dashboard request, where change control means a formal review of a proposed change before it is approved. Say what Dana should not do.
3. Choose a risk response for the vendor delay, where a risk is a possible future event and a risk response is the planned action taken about it. Name the response you choose from avoid, transfer, mitigate, or accept, explain it in your own words, and explain how the delay would be handled differently if it had already happened, which would make it an issue.
subParts: Choosing waterfall or agile for each part
Change control for the dashboard request
Risk response for the vendor delay
modelAnswer: Fixed-standard hardware installation with a fixed delivery date suits waterfall, because the requirements are known in advance, the sequence of steps matters, and changing the plan late is costly. The software build suits agile, because its requirements are likely to change as warehouse staff use early versions, and short sprints with feedback let the team adjust. A strong answer gives a sensible reason for each choice, not just a label.

Dana should log the dashboard request in a change request, assess its effect on scope, schedule, cost, and quality, and take it to the change control board or the designated approver for a decision before any work starts. She should not add the dashboard to the current sprint on her own authority or let the team start building it informally, because that bypasses the review and can silently delay other work. A strong answer names a formal review and an approval before work begins.

Mitigate or transfer are both defensible, but the best answer chooses one and justifies it: for example, mitigate by asking the vendor for earlier shipping updates and identifying a backup supplier or a temporary plan for installing scanners in phases. Accept is weaker because the delay could push the fixed regulatory date. An issue is a problem that has already happened and needs immediate action, so if the shipment were already three weeks late, Dana would move from planning a response to actively fixing the impact, such as escalating and rescheduling. A strong answer distinguishes a possible future event from a current problem.

scenarios.title: Parcel tracking portal at Brightwater Parcel Co.
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcel Co. is a fictional regional courier with about 400 staff. Its customers currently phone the call centre to ask where a parcel is, and leadership wants a customer-facing tracking page instead. Three weeks ago, project manager Priya Nkemelu ran a discovery workshop. Discovery is the early stage where the team investigates the real problem, talks to users and lists possible options before committing money. The workshop produced a problem statement, a one-page description of the pain point, and a list of three options. Last week the operations director, who acts as sponsor, signed a project charter. A project charter is the formal document that authorizes the project, names the project manager and sets a budget ceiling. The team is now writing a work breakdown structure, which splits the deliverables into smaller pieces of work, and a schedule. No work on the web page has started yet. Answer the following: 1. Name the phase the project is in right now, and the artifact that phase is producing. 2. Explain what the discovery workshop output was for, and why the team should keep it after the charter is signed. 3. At the end of the project, name the phase that handles handover to operations, and the artifact that records what was delivered and what was learned.
modelAnswer: The project is in the planning phase. Planning is where the team turns the authorized idea into a detailed written approach covering scope, the work breakdown structure, schedule, budget and risks. Its main artifacts are the project management plan and baselines. A baseline is an approved reference version of scope, schedule or cost that later progress is measured against. A common mistake is calling this phase execution because the team is busy. The consequence is that if building starts before a baseline exists, the team cannot tell later whether a change was approved or simply drifted in.

Discovery is the early investigation stage that establishes the real problem before any solution is chosen. Its outputs, the problem statement and the options list, record why the project exists and which alternatives were considered. The team keeps them because the charter and plan refer back to them. When someone later asks why option B was chosen, the answer comes from the discovery record. A common mistake is treating discovery as optional and jumping straight to building a page. The consequence is that the team may build a tool that solves the wrong problem and must rework it.

The closing phase handles the formal end of the project: confirming that deliverables were accepted, handing them to operations, releasing staff and resources, and closing contracts. Its key artifacts are the formal acceptance or sign-off record, the final project report, and the lessons learned register, which is a document listing what went well and what should change next time. A common mistake is skipping lessons learned because the project appears finished. The consequence is that the next project repeats the same delays, because nobody recorded what caused them.

scenarios.title: Larkspur Dental Supplies: Choosing the Right Tool for a Struggling Order System Upgrade
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Dental Supplies is a fictional mid-sized company that sells dental equipment by mail order. Its project team is six months into replacing the old order-tracking system with a new cloud-based one. Priya Anand is the newly appointed project manager. In her first week she inherits a status report that her predecessor sent as a long email each Friday. The email says the project is 'mostly on track, with some issues.' Priya knows that vague wording hides real problems. Over the last eight weeks, the testing team logged 212 defects (errors in the software), but nobody has looked at where they cluster. Three work packages (groups of related tasks) are running late, and the dependencies between them (tasks that cannot start until another task finishes) are tracked in a spreadsheet that only the previous manager understood. The sponsor wants a clear picture before the steering meeting on Thursday, and the team lead wants a tool the whole team can update daily. Priya must choose tools and charts rather than rely on another status email.

Answer the following:

1. Priya wants to show the sponsor which kinds of defects cause most of the problems so the team can fix the biggest causes first. Name the chart that fits this purpose and explain why it suits it better than a simple total or a line chart of weekly defect counts.

2. The team lead needs a way to see every task, its owner, its start and finish dates, and which tasks depend on which. Name the tool or chart that fits this need and explain how it shows dependencies and schedule slippage that a plain list cannot.

3. Priya needs a shared place where the team writes meeting notes, the decision log, and the risk register, and where everyone can see the latest version without emailing attachments back and forth. Name the type of tool that fits this need and explain why it beats emailing documents.
subParts: Chart for ranking defect causes by share of total problems
Tool for showing tasks, owners, dates and dependencies
Shared productivity tool for notes, logs and the risk register
modelAnswer: A Pareto chart is the right choice. It is a bar chart where the defect categories are sorted from largest to smallest, with a cumulative line showing the running share of the total. It works because it shows which few causes account for most of the defects, following the common pattern that a small share of causes produces most of the problems, so the team can focus effort where it pays off. A simple total only gives one number, and a weekly line chart shows when defects happened but not what caused them. For example, if the 212 defects are grouped into categories such as data import, login, and pricing rules, sorting the bars might show that data import alone accounts for about 60 percent. The cumulative line would then show that the top two categories cover most of the defects, which tells the sponsor where to act first. A common mistake is to sort the bars in random or alphabetical order, which hides the message. If the categories are not sorted, the chart looks like any other bar chart and the sponsor cannot see the priority.

A Gantt chart is the right choice. It is a timeline bar chart in which each task is drawn as a bar from its start date to its finish date, with the owner's name shown beside it. Dependencies are drawn as links between bars, so a delay in one task visibly pushes the bars that depend on it. This matters because a plain list shows dates but not the chain reaction. For example, if the data migration task (owner: Chen) finishes three days late, and the pricing test task depends on it, the link shows the test bar must move, and the critical path (the longest chain of dependent tasks that sets the earliest finish date for the project) now ends later. A common mistake is to draw the chart once at the start and never update it, so it shows a plan rather than the current state. Tools such as Microsoft Project are one example of this kind of scheduling tool; the generic idea is a shared schedule with dependencies that updates as dates change.

A shared document workspace with version history and access controls is the right type of tool. It is an online collaboration tool where one copy of each document lives in one place, several people can edit it, and the system keeps prior versions so changes can be traced and reversed. Examples include SharePoint or Google Workspace, but the generic idea is what matters. It beats emailing attachments because emailed copies multiply: each person ends up with a different version, and nobody is sure which one is current. For example, if the risk register is attached to a Friday email and two people edit their own copies, the team has two conflicting registers by Monday. In a shared workspace there is one register, the edit history shows who changed which risk and when, and the steering committee always opens the same file. A common mistake is to treat the workspace as a dumping ground with no structure, so nobody can find the decision log. Keeping a clear folder layout and a named owner for each document prevents this.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Logistics: moving delivery-address data to a new scheduling platform
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Logistics Ltd is a fictional parcel delivery company with customers in the UK and the European Union. Its project manager, Priya, is leading a six-month project to move the delivery scheduling system from an old on-premises server to a cloud-hosted scheduling platform. The new platform is run by a third-party provider. The move includes copying about 400,000 customer records, each with a name, home address, phone number and delivery notes. Priya must make sure the project follows the company's governance rules. Governance means the set of policies, approval steps and controls that decide how IT work is planned, approved and kept safe. Three issues have come up. First, the team wants to copy every field in the old database, including a date-of-birth field that no current delivery process uses. Second, the provider wants administrator access to the new system, and the team lead proposes giving every developer the same full admin login so that work is not held up. Third, a late-stage fix to the address-matching code must go live before the next weekend because of a known fault, and the developer wants to deploy it directly without waiting for the normal approval meeting. Answer the following. 1. Explain which data-protection principle applies to the date-of-birth field and what Priya should ask the team to do with it. 2. Explain what access model Priya should use for the developers and the provider, and why the shared full admin login is a problem. 3. Explain how Priya should handle the emergency address-matching fix so that it follows IT change control, and name one step she should record.
subParts: Privacy: data minimisation for the date-of-birth field
Information security: least-privilege access for developers and provider
IT change control: handling the urgent fix
modelAnswer: Personal data means any information that can identify a living person. The key principle here is data minimisation, which means collecting, copying and keeping only the personal data that a stated purpose actually needs. The date-of-birth field is not used by any current delivery process, so it should not be copied into the new platform. Priya should ask the team to confirm the field has no purpose, to exclude it from the migration scope, and to record that decision in the data mapping document. If the field must be kept for a legal reason, it should be documented with that reason and protected more strictly. A common mistake is to copy everything 'just in case'. The consequence is that the company keeps personal data it has no lawful reason to hold, which increases the damage if the system is breached and can breach privacy rules.

Least privilege means each user or account gets only the access needed for their specific job, and no more. Priya should replace the shared full admin login with separate named accounts for each developer and for the provider's staff. Each account should get a role that matches its tasks, such as read-only access for reviewers and deployment rights only for release staff. Shared accounts are a problem because they remove accountability: when something changes or breaks, the company cannot tell who did it, and an attacker who obtains the shared password gets full control. Multi-factor authentication, which requires a second proof of identity such as a code from a phone, should be added to privileged accounts. Access should be reviewed on a regular schedule and removed when people leave the project.

Change control is the formal process for requesting, assessing, approving, testing and recording any change to a live IT system. Even an urgent fix should not bypass it entirely. Priya should use the documented emergency change route, which means a short, fast approval by a named person or the change advisory board (CAB), a group that reviews changes before they go live. The change request should describe the fault, the fix, the expected impact, the testing completed, and a rollback plan, which is a tested way to return the system to its previous state if the fix fails. One step she must record is the approval, with the approver's name and time, along with the rollback plan. Skipping this record means the company cannot prove the change was authorised, and if the fix causes a fault, nobody can quickly see what changed or how to undo it.
